367.t: Al Killian and the high-note man in Lunceford's band
367.s: Young remembers Al Killian as a great high-note player who died young, and a Lunceford high-note trumpeter on Rhythm Is Our Business.
367.q: Al Killian. Al Killian, we lost him, I know him. I didn‘t work with him, but I know him. Al Killian, he was a great high note trumpet player, he was a great high note trumpet player. It‘s too bad that he died when he did, because he didn‘t get the reputation that he should have got, because he…

367.t: Freddie Hubbard's sound and his needling about the Tonight Show
367.s: Young praises Hubbard's beautiful tone, says bad habits ruined his chops, and recalls Hubbard teasing that he could do the Tonight Show job.
Young remembers Fats Navarro as a great player with range who died young before becoming widely known.
367.q: Yeah, well see, I knew he went away from here very young. And he was a big guy too. He wasn‘t little or anything. I forgot how he went away from here, its too bad he went away but he was a great trumpet player. He didn‘t get to be great, he died before people got to know him. But he had it, but he…

367.s: Young knows the name Woody Shaw but not his playing and thinks he would have been well known had he lived.
367.q: Yeah, he was a good, if he had lived he would have been well known too.

367.s: Young says Freddie Webster had a big sound, followed him into Lunceford's band, and died young from bad habits.
367.q: Freddie Webster had a good sound. Freddie Webster and I were good friends. Freddie Webster… [laughs] we kind of had a… well how was that? He followed me into Jimmie Lunceford‘s band, but he couldn‘t play what I played because he didn‘t have the sound that I had, but he had a big sound and…

367.t: The Lunceford trumpeter named Steve before Paul Webster
367.s: Young identifies Steve as the high-note trumpeter who played Rhythm Is Our Business before Paul Webster joined.
367.q: Steve was the high note trumpet player. He‘s the one that played ―Rhythm is Our Business.‖ And that kind of helped make Jimmie Lunceford famous. Steve played ―Rhythm is Our Business.‖ [Sings] ―Rhythm is our business, rhythm is what we sell. Rhythm is our business, rhythm is what we sell. Steve he‘s…

70.t: McKinney's trumpeters: Buddy Lee, John Nesbitt, Doc Cheatham and Rex Stewart
70.s: Jackson recalls Hilton Jefferson and the trumpeters of McKinney's band, including Buddy Lee as swing first trumpet, Nesbitt as arranger, and Rex Stewart's false fingering.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: -- but I knew him very well, you know. And there was a lot of great trumpet players that I played with that I could tell you --

70.s: Paul Webster replaced Tommy Stevenson in Lunceford's band and could play any high note; Hinton calls him the black Clark Gable.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, he was wonderful, a wonderful trumpet player. But Paul could play -- I don't care how high it was, Paul would play it, --

70.t: High-note trumpeters: Tommy Stevenson, Al Killian and Shad Collins
70.s: He praises Tommy Stevenson's altissimo with Lunceford, Al Killian's range in Redman's band, and underrated Shad Collins.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Then, of course, I can go down to -- in the thirties I played with Al Killian Kahan in Don's band. Al Kahan was playing high notes before Maynard Ferguson or any of those guys. In fact, there was one trumpet player before him, even, Tommy Stevenson, that was with the original Jimmy Lunceford…

70.t: Rex Stewart's tricks, appetite and reading
70.s: Rex Stewart had many tricks and false fingerings, a big appetite and a good ear that covered slow reading; Jackson played with him in McKinney's band.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: many tricks and he was fast, very fast. You know, that's who Roy listened to in the beginning. That's who Roy kind of patterned after to adopt his style, you see. And Rex used to cover the valves up -- he would finger his horn and cover the valves up and use a lot of false fingering so the guys…

70.t: Bobby Stark and Chick Webb's trumpet section
70.s: Stark was neat, quiet and one of the cleanest trumpeters; Jackson praises Webb's trumpets of Dick Vance, Stark and Taft Jordan.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Yeah, he wasn't too plump but he was very neat. Neat as a pin. He was immaculate. And very quiet, never had much to say, but he didn't have to with what came out of the horn.

70.t: Russell Pop Smith: the trumpeter who could not read words
70.s: Russell Smith, from Ripley, Ohio, could not read or write yet was a great first trumpeter and a sergeant in the First World War orchestra.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: That's right, one day. And he could play any kind of trumpet. He could double tongue, triple tongue and play the most beautiful melody.

418.t: Forgotten trumpet greats: Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris
418.s: He says great players like Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris are forgotten, though Rex wrote and composed.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: He could play anything. I don't know why. This is several guys -- no one -- everyone seems to forget about. There's Rex Stewart. There's another guy was a genius on the trumpet. He really was. I mean I'm not taking anything away from anybody, but you know -- he was just a great guy.

418.t: Forgotten trumpet greats: Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris
418.s: He says great players like Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris are forgotten, though Rex wrote and composed.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Yeah! Not only was he a musician, he was a writer and everything. And a composer; he wrote some... So he was a pretty good dude.

418.t: Forgotten trumpet greats: Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris
418.s: He says great players like Rex Stewart, Jabbo Smith and Sidney De Paris are forgotten, though Rex wrote and composed.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: He could play anything. I don't know why. This is several guys -- no one -- everyone seems to forget about. There's Rex Stewart. There's another guy was a genius on the trumpet. He really was. I mean I'm not taking anything away from anybody, but you know -- he was just a great guy.

418.t: Rex Stewart, Earl Hines and who gets remembered
418.s: He wonders why no one mentions Rex Stewart, a great trumpet player, and they discuss how leaders get remembered.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: They had Rex in the band. No one ever says anything about Rex! I wonder why. Rex was a great trumpet player.

418.t: Hot Lips Page and unremembered players
418.s: Lips Page is another unmentioned player, and Dickenson compares forgotten musicians to a worn-out discarded toy.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: There's another one no one ever says anything about. There are so many guys, guys that people don't say anything about. You know what I mean? They're Alas (?) and they're gone and forgotten. It's like a toy that you throwed away; it got worn out. They don't even remember that toy no more.

251.t: Sid Isles and trumpeter George Washington Smith
251.s: Albert defers to Driggs on Sid Isles and recalls George Smith, a fairly good trumpeter.
251.q: I believe Braggs could have answered that better than me. Oh. Because Braggs knew him. And I didn't hear Sid. I knew others.

251.t: Kimball, listening to whole bands, and end of the reel
251.s: Albert asks about trumpeter Kimball and Alvin Alcorn, says he listens to the whole band, and the reel ends.
251.q: This is the trumpet player. Alvin talked about him. Alvin Alcorn. I think he was, but I think he worked later on with Rosesh.

251.t: Overlooked players: Chester Clark, Fred Murphy, two Buster Baileys
251.s: Albert says historians overlook players such as Chester Clark, Mottwai, Fred Murphy and a Dallas Buster Bailey; mentions Buster Smith.
251.q: I had a good one. Like I said, Chester Clark was a very fine trumpet player, sweet trumpet player. Then there's another fellow I recall in New Orleans that I used to admire his playing and I think that a lot of the other fellows really did and all Mottwai. Oh yes.

251.s: Albert mentions Jack Willis and the Keyhole, then praises Joe Phillips, a trumpeter and arranger from his band who never talked much.
251.q: I'll tell you when Jack came in. Jack didn't work in my band. Mm-hmm. But Jack did come to San Antonio when I'd given up the band with Freddie Coleman's little band at the first keyhole nightclub that I had. Mm-hmm. But there was a fellow yesterday at the concert that they very seldom mentioned…

78.t: Shelton Hemphill: Collegians, Savoy battle, Ellington and Millinder
78.s: Hemphill, from the Birmingham school, was an excellent sight reader and pumper on trumpet in the Collegians and later played with Ellington, Millinder and Fletcher.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: : Shad Shell -- Shelton Hemphill was from Birmingham, Alabama, out of a high school that turned out quite a few great musicians from a great band leader down there -- we called him Fess Watney, and Shelton Hemphill graduated from that school, and he was an excellent reader. He had big shoulders…

78.t: Shelton Hemphill and Rex Stewart's blue notes
78.s: Shelton Hemphill came from Birmingham, later played with Ellington and Millinder. Rex Stewart played cornet in the Collegians and could sell a sour note to the Detroit crowd.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: -- Alabama, from the same school that the McCord brothers came from, and he turned out to be a great reading trumpet player. In fact, from my band he went to the great bands, like he played with Duke Ellington for quite a spell. He played with Lucky Millinder and his great band, and we called him…

78.t: Emmett Berry: underrated trumpet and how Horace used him
78.s: Berry came from Cleveland, played with Fletcher and Duke, used a Roy Eldridge-style mute, and Horace saved him for out choruses. He and Crosby were the core of the Omaha band.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: 1940. Now that's a trumpet player that, in my estimation, that, unfortunately, he didn't get his just dues as a musician. What I mean by that, he didn't have anybody to actually push him. He played in Fletcher's band for quite a long time. We found him in Cleveland, Ohio, and he was another good…

78.t: Rex Stewart: cornet, third trumpet, and selling a sour note
78.s: Rex Stewart was an aggressive ear player on third trumpet who could sell a blue note to a packed house, as at the Graystone battle; he pumped his stomach and drew laughs.
78.ch: Fletcher as a leader and early bandmates
78.q: -- but actually it was a great experience for me because they all had different personalities; yet they were great musicians, and, of course, starting out with Rex Stewart, I was fortunate enough to have Rex Stewart in my band with the Wilberforce Collegiates, along with Benny Carter.

9.t: Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Bubber Miley, Howard Scott and Cootie
9.s: He compares Newton and Coleman unfavorably to Stark's drive and praises Howard Scott's tone; the interview breaks off with Cootie Williams mentioned.
9.q: : Well, he was a good trumpet player. But there was something Frankie lacked in comparison with Bobby Stark. See, Bobby had that drive, which Frankie didn't have. Frankie was a good trumpet player.

9.s: Holmes says there was no shortage of trumpeters and none outstanding, naming Bobby Stark and Rex Stewart.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: He was a good trumpeter. He was one of the good ones. And there was a lot of them, a lot of good ones. There was never no shortage of trying to find a good trumpeter. There was Bobby Stark, we had what's his name, who used to be with Fletcher, the fat....

9.s: Holmes recalls trumpeters June Clark, who later boxed, and Ed Swayzee, a neat, clean player, but little detail about either.
9.q: : Well, I remember June Clark, but I don't remember him being with Ellington. I guess he had been. I remember June Clark...

149.t: Dud Bascomb as an underrated trumpeter
149.s: Hawkins praises Dud's ideas and notes his solo on 'Tuxedo Junction'.
149.q: And I had a lot, and I cared for his playing very much so. Cause we was, he had very beautiful ideas.

149.t: Hot Lips Page and Charlie Spivak
149.s: He calls Page a 100 percent trumpeter and credits Spivak for his sweet playing.
149.q: Yeah. That's, that was another old buddy of mine too. Yeah, he was 100 percent. I just happened to come back when he brought back Dud. I met him when I was down at 'Bama State, and then after that in New York. Yeah, a 100 percent trumpet player. And he had beautiful ideas. The same, you know, we…

149.t: Younger trumpeters: Clifford Brown, Fats Navarro, Freddie Hubbard
149.s: He admires them and notes the early deaths.
149.ch: Highlights, the reunion album and fellow musicians
149.q: Well, besides Dizzy. Now, they had a trumpet player. A young man, he died when he was 21, accident. Oh, boy. He was, he was marvelous. I believe that name may come up pretty soon.

124.t: Trumpet players who push themselves: Freddy Webster, Shavers, Eldridge
124.s: Some good trumpeters never promote themselves, unlike Charlie Shavers and Roy Eldridge, who stayed in the spotlight.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: They're there and they know they're good. It's nothing they'll do to push themselves, you know. (Inaudible). I can do this, I can do that. They don't put themselves in the spotlight to -- oh, everybody know Charlie Shavers. Charlie Shavers was something else. You know, it's the difference between…

124.s: McRae recalls trumpeter Frankie Newton, who died young, and Rudy Powell from the 14th Street band.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Frankie Newton was an outstanding trumpet player. Good recording man. He made a lot of -- I think he made a lot of recordings.

124.t: June Clark, trumpeter who lost his upper register
124.s: McRae calls Clark one of the outstanding 1930s trumpeters, once rated with Armstrong, until a split lip left him unable to play high.
124.ch: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
124.q: Evidently, he didn't wait till it healed up or it didn't heal up right or something. One of the nerves -- he was unable -- he could play, he could really play, but he was unable to hit any more high notes or go high like he used to go.

33.t: The Brunies brothers and DeDroit's trumpet style
33.s: DeDroit talks about Merritt and Abbie Brunies, being pulled on stand by one of them, and how he played trumpet with conviction.
33.ch: Other bands, mutes, arrangers and composers
33.q: I wasn't there enough to him to hear it, because I was not. They asked me, but now you've heard of the Brunese brothers, Merrick Brunus, Abby Brunus, you know one of them died.

33.t: Johnny Bayersdorffer, the best Dixieland trumpeter
33.s: He praises Johnny Bayersdorffer as his idea of a clean Dixieland trumpet, whose OKeh recordings he thinks the best, and says he never got his due.
33.q: Johnny Baisnautha died lately. Did you know that? Yes. Now there was my idea of a Dixieland trumpet. Yeah. Clean as a pen, every note, and a fine style. And I think of all the recordings that O.K. made here that Johnny Baisnautha made the best. That's my idea.

1.t: Wildest trumpet players of the era
1.s: He recalls two young trumpeters he heard in a nightclub who played like Louis Armstrong.
1.q: The wildest and most exciting time that I saw in the all, back to the wildest trumpet play I saw at that time. Most of the was Lee Collins and all of this, and boy, I heard them all. But the youngster Guy Keller came from Baton Rouge, at the same time Johnny Hander came from across the lake. And I…

1.t: Joe Smith and Pike Davis, trumpet players
1.s: Danny and Milt discuss Russell's brother Joe Smith, who mesmerized with his trumpet, and Pike Davis, a pit-band trumpeter and rival of Johnny Dunn.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Joe Smith... Well, I didn't know him either. I saw him once. He went to Kansas City with the Cotton-Pickers, McKinney's Cotton Pickers, and he met a woman out there and he stayed out there for six months. Some big sportin' woman. 'Cause he was a cat could mesmerize you with that trumpet. Joe Smith,…

621.s: Duhé calls Sugar Johnny a smooth trumpet player in the manner of Bunk.
621.q: But he's a smooth trumpet player. He's a pretty honest style of bunk. Bunkway on smooth. On the order of bunk too. Yeah, smooth, smooth trumpet player. Good morning.

621.t: Tig Chambers and his trumpet style
621.s: Duhé recalls playing with Tig Chambers, a powerful trumpeter in the style of Bunk Johnson.
621.ch: Early life and New Orleans bands
621.q: T-I-G. and he's the first to bring it out there. We used to go listening.

138.t: Comparing later cornet players; Lawrence Vega, Pacquet and Perkins
138.s: Laine praises his cornet players, saying none played the time like them; he singles out Lawrence Vega, with Pacquet and Dave Perkins.
138.q: I told Dr. Sushaw on that too. I don't like it. I don't like that music. He said, you don't. I said, no, I don't like it, doctor. I don't like it. I don't like that music.

138.t: Wrapping up: best cornet players and copying pictures
138.s: As time runs out Laine says La Rocca was not among his best cornetists, names Brunies, and Russell asks to copy the photos.
138.ch: Photo session: wagons, parades and goodbyes
138.q: He played a many job. He played a many job with me. But he didn't play very much with me. I didn't want to record. Because I had plenty of cornets players. Oh, that's all right. Oh, I had lots of cornets players.

819.t: Debating books on early New Orleans trumpeters and the Brunies family
819.s: Sbarbaro and Christian argue over what a French book says about Keppard, Perez, Vega and Lopez, and recall the Brunies brothers.
819.q: No, no. There you go. I mean, that's what I mean. You see, none of them don't mention the white trumpet player. Vega? Vega was white.

819.s: Sbarbaro judges Vega and modern high-note trumpet playing.
819.q: Vega was a good trumpet player, any way you're looking. That's a hard thing for a man like Butterfield. A fellow will say, that man can play anywhere. What could Vega do? Vega could play trumpet.

677.t: High-note trumpeters: Jenkins, Stewart, Cat Anderson, Killian
677.s: He recalls Freddie Jenkins as Little Posey, then Rex Stewart, Cat Anderson, and Al Killian.
677.ch: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
677.q: Freddie Jenkins played the high notes. We used to call him Little Posey. He was on the end. He was a small fellow and very flashy, and it seems that every man that became a member of that band had some quality that attrac-

677.t: Trumpeters Shorty Baker and Ray Nance
677.s: Baker was among the best, applauded at Carnegie Hall; Nance was a multi-talented violinist and singer whose A Train chorus became a model.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: she was with, you know, and then he came with us, finally. And I remember distinctly one of his terrific things he did was on a transitional phrase, I think it was, "Black, Brown and Beige." Which he played all by himself, in no time, you know, just played and it was so terrific that at the concert…

0.t: Fletcher's Roseland band, Joe Smith and Howard Scott
0.s: He lists men in Fletcher Henderson's Roseland band and admires Joe Smith's muted style, shared only by Howard Scott.
0.ch: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
0.q: That's true. They were the first call him Smack colored band in the Roseland Ballroom, and we'd go and inspect for (unintelligible) short -- that was the nickname. And Smack got all them fellows, Buster and Don Redmon, Coleman Hawkins, Joe Smith. You know, Joe had three brothers. See, there's about…

0.t: Ward Pinkett as friend and roommate
0.s: Caldwell and Ward Pinkett were buddies; Pinkett was a nice trumpeter of part Indian descent who stayed with the group.
0.ch: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
0.q: He was a nice trumpet player, and through the years -- on his mother's side was part Indian, like my -- my great-grandfather was an old Indian chief. And Ward could pass, but he wouldn't. And like the bands, like with the (unintelligible) rumba bands at the time was bigger, late the time, in the…

169.s: McGhee praises Harriet Calloway's trumpeter Charlie Jacobs as modern as Roy Eldridge with a beautiful tone, and tells how he fell apart when she left.
169.q: : Charlie Jacobs, right. He was a helluva trumpet player, too, man. I used to marvel at this cat every night. Every time he played he was somethin' else.

169.s: He credits Webster as the real 'Stardust' player, with an unmatched sound.
169.ch: Bird's world, singers and the new music
169.q: : Well, I heard Freddie Webster play "Stardust," and I really didn't want to play "Stardust" no more after I heard that -- just to let you know what I thought about how he was playing. But I really didn't want to play "Stardust" no more after I heard him play it. Butt I had to, because I had played…

74.t: Peanuts: great trumpet, no tone, and his death
74.s: Peanuts played powerfully but never had a good tone; he died after saying he could not understand why he lived without playing.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: No, I know that on "After You've Gone." I wonder why he was kind of powerful in the background he wanted to take that place, if it was left up to the rest of us, he would have had it written out probably.

74.t: Peanuts's tone and his death (second version)
74.s: Peanuts played like mad but had no tone; Mosley saw him in Sweden before he died.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: They did. He was a little, short guy; he was always sensitive about being short and he wore real high heeled shoes. It looked like he was going to tip over on us. I saw him in Sweden; that was some reunion.

242.t: Favorite trumpeter Roy Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie
242.s: Roy Eldridge is his favorite trumpeter; he and his son debate Eldridge and Dizzy Gillespie.
242.q: I mean, I was playing that well, I mean, over men, you know? See? But like I said, I mean, I was copying those records. Following behind Louis Armstrong and this guy and that guy, see? But up until today, my favorite trumpet player is Roy Eldridge. That's my favorite, you know? Because my son and I…

174.s: Dejan describes Kimball, a good trumpeter and headman, who went to Shreveport.
174.ch: Dance jobs and the opera house
174.q: He's heard the name, yeah. Oh, when he left here, he went to Shreveport. We had to start the end in Shreveport. That's where I met him. I met him around here once or twice, but last I seen him, that's where he was at, and he's not where he was dead.

35.t: Mutt Carey's lead, vibrato and tone compared with Bunk and Kid Thomas
35.s: Blumberg met Mutt only once or twice, says his lead was looser than Bunk's authoritative one, and compares his fast vibrato to Kid Thomas's; the talk continues on trumpet tone into reel 2.
35.q: I think, I just probably heard him once or twice, maybe, around New York, and his lip was kind of out of shape, you know.

769.t: Favorite trumpeter and Elmer Talbert's early career
769.s: His favorite for authentic jazz was Herb Morand; he recalls hearing Talbert on advertising trucks before he joined Lewis.
769.q: Yeah. Yeah. Because I saw him several times on that Voilishman's. Uh, playing for different dancers. Mm-hmm. He'd even sing on that truck without a mic. Yeah. Oh, man. Yeah, that was long before he had started playing with John up with us. Yeah. As he had joined up with us back as manager. See,…

246.t: Trumpeters Edward Clem, Ned; Wooden Joe's nickname; Lawrence Toca
246.s: Glass doesn't remember Clem, explains that Joe Nicholas was nicknamed Wooden Joe for his hard playing, and mentions Toca.
246.q: Yeah. Never know a trumpet player by the name of Ned. I don't know if his last name or first name. Ned, they called him. No. I might know him by her name, you know. I heard that. I heard that. Because you see, all of them had different, they had nicknames. Like we give Wooden Joe, Wooden Joe. He's…

862.s: George McCullum was the outstanding trumpet soloist for hymns and dirges, a clean player who did not blast.
862.q: Yeah. George McCulloch. That's one of the guys that nobody did 90 years ago. They used to fit him all the time. Any hot thing coming, the King Madras and things. They didn't come back. The boy gets back. He's been a little bit further. He's been trouble with that.

999.t: Favorite horn players: Kid Rene and Kyfer
999.s: Jones paid attention mainly to drummers, but admired trumpeters Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and Kyfer.
999.ch: Other drummers and New Orleans musicians
999.q: Well, just like I've always told you, I wasn't too much interested in other guys in the band. All I was interested in was the drumming. Drumming was the only thing I was interested in.

178.t: Buddy Petit, Ferbos's own trumpet style, and Gaudet
178.s: Asked whether he sounded like the older trumpeters, Ferbos says his style has changed; Dejan places him with the musically able Perez-type players, and they mention Gaudet.
178.q: Well I mean the fellas we had first started to talk about. Now I didn't know him personally, but I heard Buddy Petit several times on these parades, you know, but I didn't know him personally.

180.s: He names Pete Lacarre, Kid Punch and Kid Rainey as trumpeters he admired.
180.q: Well my favorite trumpet players was one, I'll tell you, one fella I admired for the style of playing. Pete Lacarre was one, see. I also admired Kid Punch. That's another one. Kid Punch and Pete Lacarre. I'll tell you another fella too, I admired playing too, was Kid Rainey. Kid Rainey I admired…

259.t: Trumpet players and plunger mute specialists
259.s: Favorite trumpeters include Oliver, Guy Kelly and Buddy Petit; Chris Kelly was best with the plunger mute.
259.q: So what about the trumpet players? In the outside, Joe Oliver and Guy Kelly and, let's see, Prince. What about Buddy Petit? Yeah, Buddy Petit. Yeah, Buddy Petit. Yeah, I think Buddy Petit died, you know. Buddy used to get drunk so much, you know. But I always liked his playing. Yeah, Buddy was…

32.t: Georgia Smart Set, Bunk Johnson and White's own featured solos
32.s: White recalls Bunk Johnson on the Georgia Smart Set and describes his own New Orleans-style features and triple-tongue solos.
32.q: So, you can tell me a little bit about it. Well, Buck, Buck served the season on the, on the Georgia Smart Set, uh, under Frank Moreland. Uh, and Buck was a featured man in the way he played. And Buck was a very fine jazz man. And he had a distinct way of, of playing the special numbers that Frank…

955.t: Favorite trumpeters: Keppard, Bunk, and sweet versus straight styles
955.s: He recalls hearing Oliver talk, Freddie Keppard and Bunk Johnson at the Entertainers, and contrasts sweet players like Metoyer with Perez.
955.q: No, in the city. It was a colored nightclub. They called the Entertainers. Anormatwai was working there. He used to go there and wrestle Anormatwai after, you know, he gets off a job here. And everybody would be hollering for him. Bunk, play a number. Play a number, Bunk. But you know he always…

182.t: Best cornet players when Tom was young
182.s: Tom names the best old-time cornetists, Naum Manetta, George Moret, Picou and others, why they were good, and Dude who played in the district; the reel ends garbled.
182.q: When I was young, old man. Now, the best cornet player was Nauman and Fess's uncle. And then the old man used to lead that band, Verrett. George? George Verrett and Emmanuel coming after them. Them were all the best cornet players at the time. So, Lizard, them, they could play, you know, but they…

474.t: Del P's, Bama and blues trumpet
474.s: Meeting Albert Delon, Bama, Papa Toot at Del P's; Bama's blues trumpet and scarcity of such players.
474.q: Sure. And why I really got interested and got a lot of experience is that Del P, Del P's. That's when I met Albert DeLon playing saxophone, trumpet player by the name of Bama, and Papa Toot.

724.t: Trumpeters McLeod, Leonard Parker, Dan Moody and Lee Collins
724.s: Trumpet players he worked with, comparing Moody to Lee Collins and noting Collins played second trumpet in the Elite band.
724.q: There was a Trump McLeod from Slidell. He used to play with a lot too. He used to work through Mississippi and he used to send for Samuel Penn and I. Thomas Parker, you ever heard of? Leonard Parker. Leonard Parker. You ever heard of Leonard Parker? Sure, George Lewis used to play with him. I know…

826.s: They try to recall early players including Joe Johnson and a trumpeter nicknamed Ned who played with Buddy.

921.t: Microphone photo and his sweet trumpet tone
921.s: Looking at a band photo with a possible microphone, they praise his sweet tone, like Harry James, as if singing.

969.s: Dick and Red Mackey, young white cornetists modeled on Emmett Hardy, and Monk Hazel as the source on Hardy and the Boswells.
969.ch: New Orleans dance scene of the 1920s

764.t: Galveston pianists, the Seven Aces and Houston trumpeters
764.s: Manno covers Jack Sharp, Albert Anderson and the Seven Aces, then Houston trumpeters including Vic Ensurello, Benny Bell, Kit Reed and Neil Hoard.

273.s: Jones likes Fazola, Pete Fountain and all styles, and says Harry James's band was his first interest.

I mean, I like all styles of music as far as that. All the different types, modern jazz, you know, Dixieland, old jazz. It all was…

569.t: Favorite trumpeters: Kid Rena, Kid Howard, Elmer Talbot
569.s: He names his favorite trumpet players and describes Kid Rena's strong tone and chops.

Kid Renee, yeah, I think he was great. And another boy is very good too. He's nice, he had a kind of stroke…

631.t: Laine's trumpeters, Vega, and Willie Guitar

He had several trumpet players and well enough to make four or five bands. And instead of giving one man all…

664.t: Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Punch Miller as trumpet men
664.s: He ranks Punch, Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Rene above today's players, praising Sam Morgan's tone and head arrangements.
664.q: I don't think there's any of them today can touch Sam Morgan Buddy Petit Rene, Punch Punch was a powerful trumpet man Man, when he was in his prime Dickie blew an ant off a horn I don't believe you heard him when he was in his prime

776.q: Not particularly. They didn't use this too much. In fact, Dewey Jackson played much too loud. He was a loud type and featured himself a great deal. And that was one of the drawbacks. He did play pretty loud, Dewey Jackson did.

8.s: Garland names Alvin Alcorn, Blakeney and Teddy Buckner, whom he brought into the Ory band.
